## Introduction

R makes it remarkably easy to fit a multivariate linear model. You don't need a special
function. You just give `lm()` a matrix of responses instead of a single one:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
fit <- lm(cbind(mpg, qsec) ~ hp + wt, data = mtcars)
class(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "mlm" "lm" 
```


:::
:::


<!--
mtcars is just for the hook: two responses, fuel economy and quarter-mile time.
A better-motivated example (Rohwer? iris? NeuroCog?) can take over in the package
sections. Or use one dataset throughout?
-->

The result is an object of class `"mlm"` that *also* inherits from `"lm"`. That second
class is a promise, or at least a hope: anything that works for a linear model should work
here too. So, as you would for any regression, you ask for the diagnostic plots:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
plot(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error:
! 'plot.mlm' is not implemented yet
```


:::
:::


Well, that's honest, at least. Other functions fail less gracefully. Several old friends from
the `car` package stop with messages that tell you nothing about why:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
car::avPlots(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error in `complete.cases()`:
! not all arguments have the same length
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
car::vif(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error in `if (names(coefficients(mod)[1]) == "(Intercept)") ...`:
! argument is of length zero
```


:::
:::


The more interesting cases are the ones that ***don't* fail**, but don't give you anything **useful**:
`cooks.distance()` runs without a
murmur and gives you a Cook's D for each case, separately for each response:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
head(cooks.distance(fit), 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                        mpg         qsec
Mazda RX4      1.589652e-02 0.0454756076
Mazda RX4 Wag  5.464779e-03 0.0280809974
Datsun 710     2.070651e-02 0.0003741428
Hornet 4 Drive 4.724822e-05 0.0051368087
```


:::
:::


That's two **univariate** answers to what was a **multivariate** question: which cases have an undue
influence on the model as a whole? 

* `summary(fit)` does the same thing, returning a list of
separate regression summaries, one per response, as if you'd called `lm()` twice. 
* Nothing
warns you that the correlation between the responses, which is the whole point of fitting
them together, has dropped out of the analysis. 

The question of _multivariate influence_
is now largely solved in my [`mvinfluence`](https://friendly.github.io/mvinfluence/) package, which was part of my learning curve
for the larger question I'm addressing here.

In short, the multivariate linear model is **easy to fit** yet **hard to see**. 

* The *model syntax* extension in `lm()` is trivial & expressive:^[For this we can
  thank @WilkinsonRogers1973. Their symbolic notation for ANOVA models, which came to R by way of
  GenStat, GLIM and S, helped reduce a whole pantheon of functions and programs for special
  cases ($t$-tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, regression, ...) to one God Formula Notation,
  `response ~ terms`.] `y` becomes `cbind(y1, y2, ...)`. You only need to
  understand the idea of **"binding"** rows or columns into a matrix. But `cbind()` and `rbind()`
  also work for a sequence of vectors, matrices and dataframes. The same formula language
  stretches further in the relatives of `lm()`: `|` indicates *grouping* or *conditioning* in
  **lme4** and **lattice**, and `glm()` adds `family =` for non-Gaussian responses. It's easy
  to think of all these as one general class, and write the model syntax without breaking a sweat.
  
* The _matrix algebra_ extension is elegant & beautiful:
  $\mathbf{y}_{n \times 1} \rightarrow \mathbf{Y}_{n \times q}$ --- it largely just works!
  
  -  The residual variance $\sigma^2$ becomes a covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. 
  
  - The $F$ ratio of hypothesis to error sums of squares becomes the eigenvalues of
  $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^{-1}$, which give Wilks' $\Lambda$, the Pillai trace,
  Hotelling-Lawley and their maximum friend Roy. 
  
  - And $\textrm{Var}(\widehat{\mathbf{b}}) = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}$ becomes
  $\textrm{Var}(\textrm{vec}\, \widehat{\mathbf{B}}) = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \otimes (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}$,
  where $\otimes$ is the [Kronecker product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker_product).
  
  - Once there's a covariance matrix, you can even ask whether it's the same in every group:
  Box's $\mathcal{M}$ test [@Box:1949] gives you the numbers. And once you can ask, you want to *look*:
  [`heplots::plot.boxM()`](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/reference/plot.boxM.html) draws
  $\ln |\mathbf{S}|$ as a dot for each group and one for the pooled matrix, so you see *which*
  groups stand out, not just *whether* they differ [@FriendlySigal:2018:eqcov]. But why stop
  at the determinant, when there are other ways to ask "How big is a matrix?" Ah, but that's
  another story, better left for [another chat around my multivariate fireplace](https://friendly.github.io/blog/posts/2026-11-How-big/).

## One more dimension

Why should this be so hard? The statistics of the multivariate linear model have been
settled for more than half a century. The trouble is more mundane, and I think it's worth
naming, because it explains nearly every problem I've run into in developing these ideas.

It calls to mind the cognitive problems "A. Square" encountered in Edwin Abbott's
_Flatland_ [@Abbott:1884], when a Sphere entered the story and taught him how to think in
one more dimension. I've told that story in my [_Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in R_](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/) book [@Friendly:2024:VisMLM]. 

::: {.precept}
[The Gospel of One More Dimension]{.precept-title}
In R, when the response goes from a vector **y** to a matrix **Y**,
every object the model produces **gains a dimension**.
[Upward, not Northward]{.precept-motto}
:::

A. Square saw the light and was saved, though preaching this Gospel landed him in prison,
without a single convert. Even the Sphere, who had scoffed at a *fourth* dimension as
"utterly inconceivable", later repented and was saved. In R, salvation comes one rung at a time:

* a **scalar becomes a vector**. The residual $e_i$ for case $i$ becomes a vector
  $\mathbf{e}_i$ of $q$ residuals, one for each response. Some scalars jump two rungs at
  once: the residual variance $\sigma^2$ becomes a $q \times q$ covariance matrix
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, because along with $q$ variances it picks up the covariances between
  every pair of responses.
  
* a **vector becomes a matrix**. The coefficients $\mathbf{b}$ become a $p \times q$ matrix
  $\mathbf{B}$, and the residuals become an $n \times q$ matrix $\widehat{\mathbf{U}}$.
  
* a **matrix becomes a 3-way array**, or a list of matrices, or a tensor in some households.
  A table of confidence intervals
  for the coefficients ($p \times 2$) becomes $p \times 2 \times q$. The standard errors of
  the fitted values also jump two rungs: a vector with one number per case becomes an
  $n \times q \times q$ array, a $q \times q$ matrix for every case. That's where things
  begin to get hairy for a developer.

responses.

That extra dimension shows up first in what a function *returns*, and then in every method that
has to consume it: `print()`, `summary()`, `confint()`, `predict()`, and of course `plot()`.

Code written for one shape is handed the next one up, and it has to do *something* with it.
The challenge has always been to make that something **useful** in a multivariate context.


Base R takes several different approaches. Sometimes it simply returns the bigger object:
`coef(fit)` is the $3 \times 2$ matrix you'd expect. Sometimes it **flattens** the extra
dimension away. `confint()` strings the responses and coefficients together into one long
list of intervals:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
confint(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

mpg:(Intercept)  33.95738245 40.49715778
mpg:hp           -0.05024078 -0.01330512
mpg:wt           -5.17191604 -2.58374544
qsec:(Intercept) 17.45146289 20.19970760
qsec:hp          -0.03507046 -0.01954879
qsec:wt           0.39771199  1.48535274
```


:::
:::


The `broom` package does much the same thing in tidy form, stacking the responses in a
long data frame with a `response` column. That's perfectly convenient for a table, but in both
cases the answers for `mpg` and `qsec` sit side by side as if they had nothing to do with
each other.

And sometimes R just **refuses**, as it currently does for `predict()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
predict(fit, newdata = mtcars[1:2, ], se.fit = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error in `predict.mlm()`:
! the 'se.fit' argument is not yet implemented for "mlm" objects
```


:::
:::


I have some sympathy for that last one. 

* For a univariate model, the standard error of a
predicted value is a single number, and a confidence interval is a pair of numbers, `lwr` and
`upr`. 

* For an `mlm`, the uncertainty of each predicted point is a $q \times q$ covariance
matrix, and the natural confidence region is an *ellipse* (an ellipsoid when $q > 2$) around it. What should `predict()` return? How should it print? There's no column in
`cbind(fit, lwr, upr)` for an ellipse. Work on this is still unfinished in `heplots`
(`dev/pred.mlm.R`).

> scalar, and then find a way to see it. Most often, as it turns out, that way is an ellipse.

Over the past twenty years or so I've been filling these gaps, one package at a time, often
with John Fox and Georges Monette, who have been my inspirations in most of this work.
Importantly here, they also helped fill in gaps in my understanding of software design in R, and of thinking multivariately with geometry and graphs
[e.g., @FoxFriendlyMonette:09:compstat; @Friendly-etal:ellipses:2012; @FoxFriendlyWeisberg:13:rjournal].

Each one of these was a special case of the same problem: deciding what the extra dimension means, for the
statistics and for the software. 

### Un-Vized Problems

But, "filling the gaps" has a larger meaning for me. In data visualization,
an over-arching motivation has been to pay attention to **Un-Vized Problems**:
those for which the statistical machinery is largely developed, but which
haven't been implemented in software to help you see, understand, and
communicate your results.[^tukey59]
That's also a path I took in working on visualizing categorical data
[e.g., @Friendly:94a; @Friendly:99:EMD; @Friendly:00:VCD; @FriendlyMeyer:2016:DDAR].

[^tukey59]: To paraphrase @Tukey:59, the "practical power" of any statistical method
is the product of its statistical power, times the probability that anyone can or will
actually use it.

The sections below take the packages in turn. For each one, the questions are the same:

* what does it take to carry these methods one more dimension?
* how can a univariate display be re-imagined to show relationships among responses?


## Seeing the tests: HE plots

In a univariate linear model, every $F$ test compares two sums of squares: $SS_H$ for the
hypothesis and $SS_E$ for error. In the multivariate model, each of these becomes a
$q \times q$ matrix of sums of squares and products: $\mathbf{H}$ for each term in the
model, and one $\mathbf{E}$ for error. $\mathbf{E} = \widehat{\mathbf{U}}^\top \widehat{\mathbf{U}}$
is the sums of squares and products of the residuals,
$\widehat{\mathbf{U}} = \mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}$. All four multivariate test statistics are
functions of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^{-1}$, the matrix analog of
$SS_H / SS_E$.

That's the matrix ($\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^{-1}$) that plays the role of the scalar ($F$).
The way to see it is the **HE plot**
[@Friendly:07:manova; @FoxFriendlyMonette:09:compstat]: draw $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ as
ellipses in the space of two responses. The $\mathbf{E}$ ellipse shows the size and shape
of the residual variation. The $\mathbf{H}$ ellipse for a term shows the variation of the
fitted values due to that term. With the default "evidence" scaling, $\mathbf{H}$
protrudes outside $\mathbf{E}$ somewhere in the full response space if and only if the
term is significant by Roy's test, using its usual $F$ approximation.[^roy] (In a
two-dimensional view, the rule works only one way: outside means significant by that test,
but inside doesn't mean "not significant".)

[^roy]: This is exact when $s = \min(q, df_h) = 1$, as it is for any 1-df term. When $s > 1$,
the $F$ for Roy's test is an upper bound, so its $p$-value is too small and the visual test
is too liberal, sometimes very much so. An ellipse that pokes only a little way outside
$\mathbf{E}$ should then be checked against another test, such as Pillai's or Wilks'.

Here's an example, from Rohwer's study of how well paired-associate (PA) learning tasks
predict three aptitude and achievement tests in kindergarten children of high and low
socioeconomic status (SES). The model is a multivariate analysis of covariance: SES
is a factor, and the five PA tasks are covariates.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(heplots)
data(Rohwer, package = "heplots")
rohwer.mod <- lm(cbind(SAT, PPVT, Raven) ~ SES + n + s + ns + na + ss, data = Rohwer)
car::Anova(rohwer.mod)
```

HE plots tell most of the story of the `Anova()` table at a glance, once you know how to read them. SES and `na`
extend beyond $\mathbf{E}$, while `n`, `s` and `ss` stay well inside. `ns`, also
significant, only just reaches the edge of $\mathbf{E}$ in this view: the one-way rule at
work. The tilt of the
`Regr` ellipse shows that the PA tasks predict `SAT` and `PPVT` together, in the same
direction. 

There's also a lesson about **shape** and **dimension**. Each term with 1 df has an $\mathbf{H}$
matrix of rank 1, so its "ellipse" collapses to a line. In general, the dimension of the
$\mathbf{H}$ ellipse is the smaller of the term's df and $q$.
A factor with more than two levels (`df > 1`) gets fatter: an ellipse or ellipsoid of up to
$\min(df, q)$ dimensions, which can be filled, as well as marked with the factor means.
The Sphere knows exactly what I'm referring to here.

### What was easy

The `heplot()` functions were, honestly, the easy part, because the statistics were
already done.^[Well, "already done" is a bit glib. John Fox and I worked closely together,
  both on the details of `car::Anova()` and `linearHypothesis()` for multivariate models and
  on `heplot()`, so that each did what we both wanted for our purposes. The change logs in
  the source code tell the story: the first entry in `heplot.R` is John's (January 2007), and
  his December 2009 changes to `Anova.mlm()` for repeated-measures designs were matched a few
  days later by mine to `heplot()` ("made it work with car 2.0"). That give and take was part
  of the beauty of our collaboration
  [see @FoxFriendlyMonette:09:compstat; @FoxFriendlyWeisberg:13:rjournal].] John Fox's `car::Anova()` computes $\mathbf{H}$ for every term, and
`car::linearHypothesis()` does so for any linear hypothesis. `Anova()` returns these as a
*list* of $q \times q$ matrices, one per term: the "list of matrices" rung of the ladder.
So `heplot.mlm()` is "only" a plot method on that list:

* choose two (or three) responses and take the corresponding submatrices of
  $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{E}$;
* scale them (by the error df, and for evidence scaling, by the critical value of Roy's
  test);
* draw each one as an ellipse, using its Cholesky factor to transform a circle.

Everything that `Anova()` can test, `heplot()` can draw, including repeated-measures
designs through its `idata` and `idesign` arguments [@Friendly:2010:repeated]. And because `heplot()` is an S3
generic, anything that inherits from `"mlm"` gets an HE plot for free.

The same S3 design principle in R gave a family of graphical methods for `"mlm"` objects: `pairs()` for all pairs of
responses, `heplot3d()` for three, and `heplot1d()` for one. Other helpers came along:

* `coefplot()` shows confidence ellipses for the coefficients, generalizing
  `car::confidenceEllipse()`;
* `cqplot()` is a $\chi^2$ QQ plot of the squared Mahalanobis distances of the residuals;
* `etasq()` gives multivariate measures of effect size, and `glance()` a
  `broom`-style one-row summary for each response.

The [MANOVA](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/articles/HE_manova.html) and
[MMRA](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/articles/HE_mmra.html) vignettes have many more
examples.

### Repeated measures too!

<!-- New subsection, drafted from Friendly (2010), JSS 37(4), pp. 4-5, eqs. (6)-(9). Rework freely. -->

Repeated-measures designs come along almost for free, too. Any linear hypothesis about the
coefficients in a multivariate linear model can be written as
$\mathbf{L} \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$, where the rows of $\mathbf{L}$ pick out or contrast the
coefficients for a term. When the $q$ responses are the same measure taken over time or
conditions, the only change is a second matrix, $\mathbf{M}$, on the other side:

$$
H_0 : \mathbf{L} \mathbf{B} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{0} .
$$

$\mathbf{L}$ works on the rows of $\mathbf{B}$ and specifies the between-subject effects. The
columns of $\mathbf{M}$ are contrasts among the responses and specify the within-subject
effects. A unit vector, $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{1}$, averages over the responses, which tests the
between-subject terms. A matrix of contrasts for a within-subject factor C tests C itself
(with $\mathbf{L}$ for the intercept), and its interactions with each between-subject term.
The $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ matrices are the usual ones, computed for the transformed
responses $\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{M}$, so this is just the ordinary multivariate linear model again,
and the HE plot doesn't need to know the difference.

With two or more within-subject factors, there's nothing new to learn, just another
Kronecker product. If factor C has $c$ levels and D has $d$, with contrast matrices
$\mathbf{M}_C$ and $\mathbf{M}_D$, then

$$
(\mathbf{1}_c, \mathbf{M}_C) \otimes (\mathbf{1}_d, \mathbf{M}_D)
 = (\mathbf{1}_c \otimes \mathbf{1}_d, \;
    \mathbf{1}_c \otimes \mathbf{M}_D, \;
    \mathbf{M}_C \otimes \mathbf{1}_d, \;
    \mathbf{M}_C \otimes \mathbf{M}_D)
$$

gives the $\mathbf{M}$ matrices for the average, D, C, and the C:D interaction, in that order.
It's the same bookkeeping that builds the model matrix for a factorial design on the
between-subject side, now applied to the responses. @Friendly:2010:repeated works through
examples, including "doubly multivariate" designs, where several different measures are each
observed over the same occasions.

But this creates another data visualization challenge. The math and the code work wonderfully
here, but reading an HE plot now requires some understanding of what is encoded on each side
of $\mathbf{L} \mathbf{B} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{0}$. On the left, $\mathbf{L}$ reflects the
standard ANOVA ideas about differences among groups of subjects (the "between-S design"). On
the right, $\mathbf{M}$ reflects the differences among the responses (the "within-S design").
For a within-S term, the HE plot is drawn in the space of the transformed responses
$\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{M}$, such as the linear and quadratic trends over time, not the original
measures, so the axes themselves are contrasts.

Hierarchical, or multilevel, models solve the same problem in a different, but also elegant
way: they model the repeated measures directly, adding random effects for subjects
[@PinheiroBates:2000]. That approach burdened us with spaghetti plots, one line per subject,
but it also taught important lessons about *pooling*, how the estimates for individuals
borrow strength from the group [@EfronMorris:1977; @GelmanHill:07].[^framing]

[^framing]: There's a larger question here, about how an extension is *framed*. The classical,
univariate approach tries to account for correlated responses through special, simple cases,
such as the assumption of sphericity and the corrections for its failure. The multilevel
approach just adds another term to the model, for the random effects. That's a story for
another day.

## Seeing it in fewer dimensions: candisc

An HE plot shows two responses at a time. To see more of them, `pairs()` on an `"mlm"`
dispatches to `heplots::pairs.mlm()`, which draws the HE plot for every pair of responses,
laid out as a scatterplot matrix. That came essentially for free, from base R graphics and
S3 dispatch.[^pairs]

[^pairs]: The idea of a scatterplot matrix goes back at least to @Hartigan:75b. It has
been reworked many times since, in Trellis graphics (now **lattice**) and, for **ggplot2**,
in `GGally::ggpairs()` and other extensions.

But in an MLM there's something more:
the effect of a term doesn't have to line up with any pair of responses. The
$\mathbf{H}$ ellipsoid for a term lives in $s = \min(q, df_h)$ dimensions, in directions
that are combinations of all the responses.

The eigenvectors of $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^{-1}$ point in those directions. They define the
*canonical variates*: linear combinations of the responses that are uncorrelated within
groups, ordered by how much of the effect they capture. Their eigenvalues are the same
ones that go into the multivariate test statistics. So the canonical space is the
low-dimensional view in which the test is easiest to see.

The `Pottery` data give an example: the chemical composition (five oxides) of ancient
pottery from four sites in Britain. With $q = 5$ responses and $df_h = 3$ for `Site`, the
effect lives in $s = 3$ dimensions. `candisc()` finds them:

```{.r .cell-code}
pottery.mlm <- lm(cbind(Al, Fe, Mg, Ca, Na) ~ Site, data = Pottery)
pottery.can <- candisc(pottery.mlm)
pottery.can
```

In terms of the ladder, `candisc()` doesn't need to ignore the extra dimensions; it
*rotates* them. It finds the directions that matter for one term, and lets you ignore the
rest knowing how little you lose.

The software followed the heplots design:

* `candisc()` gets $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ from the same `car::Anova()` call, and
  returns a `"candisc"` object, for which there are `heplot()`, `heplot3d()` and `plot()`
  methods.
* There's a wrinkle: each term in the model has its own $\mathbf{H}$, and so its own
  canonical space, while $\mathbf{E}$ is shared. `candiscList()` does the analysis for
  every term at once.
* `can_lm()` goes one step further, refitting the model with the canonical scores as
  responses.
* `varOrder()` uses the angles of the structure arrows to order the responses in other
  displays, like `pairs()`, so that related variables sit together.

## Influence: mvinfluence

In the introduction, `cooks.distance(fit)` quietly gave two univariate answers, one column
per response. Load mvinfluence, and the same call gives one answer per case:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
library(mvinfluence)
D <- cooks.distance(fit)
names(D) <- rownames(mtcars)   # mvinfluence 0.9.4 names cases by row number
head(D, 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     Mazda RX4  Mazda RX4 Wag     Datsun 710 Hornet 4 Drive 
   0.052235697    0.029590855    0.023351805    0.005212763 
```


:::
:::


[The math](https://friendly.github.io/mvinfluence/reference/mvinfluence-package.html) came from @BarrettLing:92. Their generalized Cook's distance strings the
coefficient matrix out into one long vector, $\textrm{vec}(\mathbf{B})$, and measures how
far it moves when a case is deleted, in the metric of its covariance matrix. That metric is
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}$: the Kronecker
product again. As in the univariate case, $D_i$ is proportional to the product of a leverage
component and a residual component. Leverage depends only on $\mathbf{X}$, so it doesn't
change. The residual is now a vector, $\mathbf{e}_i^\top$, the $i$th row of
$\widehat{\mathbf{U}}$, so its size becomes
$q_{ii} = \mathbf{e}_i^\top \mathbf{E}^{-1} \mathbf{e}_i$, a hat value for the residuals: one
more scalar that has become a quadratic form, and in the same $\mathbf{E}$ as the HE plot.

Is the multivariate version worth the trouble? @Barrett:2003 gave a toy example, with one
predictor and two nearly identical responses, that makes the case:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
Toy <- data.frame(
  x  = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 10),
  y1 = c(0.10, 1.90, 1.00, 2.95, 2.10, 4.00, 2.95, 4.95, 10.00),
  y2 = c(0.10, 1.80, 1.00, 2.93, 2.00, 4.10, 3.05, 4.93, 10.00)
)
Toy.mlm <- lm(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x, data = Toy)
data.frame(D1  = cooks.distance(lm(y1 ~ x, data = Toy)),
           D2  = cooks.distance(lm(y2 ~ x, data = Toy)),
           D12 = cooks.distance(Toy.mlm)) |> round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     D1    D2   D12
1 0.121 0.118 0.125
2 0.124 0.103 0.298
3 0.090 0.089 0.091
4 0.083 0.082 0.083
5 0.055 0.067 0.182
6 0.069 0.085 0.232
7 0.079 0.065 0.203
8 0.066 0.064 0.069
9 0.002 0.008 3.225
```

Case 9, at $x = 10$, has high leverage, but it lies right on the line for each response, so

[vignette](https://friendly.github.io/mvinfluence/articles/uni-vs-multi.html) works
through this example in detail.

### Design challenges

Barrett & Ling's measures go further than single cases. They're defined for deleting any
*subset* $I$ of $m$ cases, which matters because pairs of influential cases can mask each
other, or have a joint influence far beyond their individual ones [@Lawrence:95].
For a subset, the leverage and residual quantities $\mathbf{H}_I$ and $\mathbf{Q}_I$ are
$m \times m$ matrices. That's the ladder once more, and it set the design:

* **The structure follows stats.** As `influence.lm()` calls `lm.influence()`,
  `influence.mlm()` is a thin wrapper around `mlm.influence()`, which does the work, for
  subsets of any size: `mlm.influence(fit, m = 2)` gives all pairs of cases. With
  `hatvalues()` and `cooks.distance()` methods for `"mlm"`, the familiar generic functions
  just work.
* **The results are lists of matrices**, one for each of the $\binom{n}{m}$ subsets. To
  plot or sort them, you need a scalar, so the functions take an argument `FUN`, either
  `det()` or `tr()`, for the "size" of each matrix. For $m = 1$, the two agree.
* **Each subset is refit directly.** The coefficients and residuals for each deleted subset
  come from direct matrix calculation, rather than from the QR decomposition that
  `lm.influence()` uses. That's simple, but the number of subsets grows quickly with $m$.
* **Barrett & Ling unify many measures** (Cook's $D$, DFFITS, and others) as the trace or
  determinant of products like
  $\mathbf{H}_I \mathbf{Q}_I (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H}_I - \mathbf{Q}_I)^a (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H}_I)^b$.
  Computing these needs powers of matrices, so the package has `mpower()` and a `%^%`
  operator.

## Robustness: robmlm()

For a univariate model, `MASS::rlm()` gives a robust fit, downweighting cases with large
residuals. Give it a matrix response, and it stops with "incompatible dimensions".

The algorithm for a multivariate version, `heplots::robmlm()`, is short. It's iteratively
reweighted least squares, with one change, which is the ladder again. In `rlm()`, a case's
weight depends on the size of its residual, $|e_i| / s$, a scalar. Here the residual is a
vector, so its size becomes a squared Mahalanobis distance, $\mathbf{e}_i^\top
\mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{e}_i$, using a robust estimate of the residual covariance matrix
$\mathbf{S}$ from `MASS::cov.trob()`. Bisquare weights are computed from these distances,
with a cutoff from the $\chi^2_q$ distribution, and the model is refit by weighted least
squares until the coefficients stop changing.

### What took more work

The harder part was making the result a full citizen of the `"mlm"` world. A `robmlm`
object has class `c("robmlm", "mlm", "lm")`, so `car::Anova()`, `heplot()` and the rest
should accept it. But the weights got in the way. Ask base R for the covariance matrix of a
weighted `mlm`, and it refuses:
`'mlm' objects with weights are not supported`. So heplots provides its own
`vcov.mlm()`, which takes the weights into account.

That works, but it's a sharp tool. Once heplots is loaded, its method replaces the one in
**stats** for *every* `"mlm"` object, not just robust ones. It gives the same answers when
there are no weights, but it's the kind of design choice I'd think twice about today.
Smaller things came later. `robmlm()` now has a method for an `mlm` object, so you can
write `robmlm(mod)` instead of repeating the formula and data, and it stores its call, so
`update()` works.

Then there were the visualizations. What does a robust fit change, and how can you see
it? `plot()` for a `robmlm` object shows the final weights for each case. Overlaying the HE
plots for the classical and robust fits shows what the downweighting does to the test.
Here it is for the `Pottery` model from the candisc section.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pottery.rlm <- robmlm(pottery.mlm)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1) + 0.1)
plot(pottery.rlm, col = Pottery$Site, segments = TRUE)

heplot(pottery.mlm, variables = c("Al", "Fe"),
       col = c("blue", "blue"), fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1)
heplot(pottery.rlm, variables = c("Al", "Fe"), add = TRUE, error.ellipse = TRUE,
       col = c("red", "red"), fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Classical", "Robust"), col = c("blue", "red"),
       lty = 1:2, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

## Now: multivariate ridge regression in genridge

<!-- MF: genridge 0.8.1 was submitted to CRAN 2026-11-20. Update the wording once it's accepted. -->

The newest member of the family is in genridge, my package for visualizing ridge
regression [@Friendly:genridge:2013]. In version 0.8.1, now on
[CRAN](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=genridge), `ridge()` accepts a matrix
response, either in a formula or as an existing `mlm` fit, and returns an object of class
`"mlmridge"`. The implementation was adapted from `lm_multiv_ridge()` in the
**VARshrink** package [@R-VARshrink]. It's marked experimental, and I'd welcome comments.

The question was how to carry the graphical methods I had developed for a single
$\mathbf{y}$, where the effects of many predictors on shrinkage are seen jointly, one
dimension up, to $\mathbf{Y}$ with $q > 1$ responses.

The `schooldata` data in heplots make a good test case. For 70 schools, three measures of
student achievement (`reading`, `mathematics` and `selfesteem`) are predicted from five
measures of the schools' resources, three of which are nearly the same variable. The
collinearity is severe enough that `visit`, strongly and positively correlated with reading
and mathematics, gets negative OLS coefficients for both.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(genridge)
data(schooldata, package = "heplots")
lambda <- c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5)
sridge <- ridge(cbind(reading, mathematics, selfesteem) ~
                  education + occupation + visit + counseling + teacher,
                data = schooldata, lambda = lambda)
```
:::


### What the extra dimension doesn't change

The first thing I learned was a little deflating. With the same ridge constant $\lambda$
for every response, each column of $\widehat{\mathbf{B}}(\lambda)$ is *exactly* the
univariate ridge estimate for that response. The ridge penalty involves only
$\mathbf{X}$, so it can't borrow strength across responses. For the same reason, the
effective degrees of freedom, the shrinkage factors and the variance inflation factors
depend only on $\mathbf{X}$, and they're the same for every response.

So if you're looking only at the effects of ridge shrinkage in terms of
**bias**,
the univariate ridge trace plot is still the right display for each response. By
default, `traceplot()` for an `"mlmridge"` object draws one panel for each.[^panel] Here the
horizontal axis is the effective degrees of freedom (`X = "df"`) rather than $\lambda$. It's
easier to interpret, and because it depends only on $\mathbf{X}$, it's the same for every
response:

[^panel]: This leaves open the question of how this should be done: `for()` loops,
`apply()` or `map()` functions, faceted displays, etc.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
traceplot(sridge, X = "df")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

At the right, df = 5 is the OLS fit; shrinkage increases to the left.](index_files/figure-html/fig-school-trace-1.png){#fig-school-trace fig-alt='Three panels of coefficient against degrees of freedom, from about 2.9 to 5, for reading, mathematics and selfesteem. In each, the large coefficient for occupation falls steeply as the degrees of freedom decrease from 5. For reading and mathematics, visit is negative at 5 df and rises, crossing zero near 4 df. For selfesteem, visit stays near 4 throughout.' width=960}

:::


Not every method needs a new multivariate display. Knowing *which* ones don't is part of
the design. The important ones for `genridge` were the novel methods I implemented to show the effects of shrinkage on **precision** of the estimates of $\boldsymbol{\beta} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$ along with **bias**: 

* **covariance ellipses** for pairs of coefficients: `plot()` and `pairs()` draw the
  confidence ellipse of $(\beta_j, \beta_k)$ for each $\lambda$, so the bias (centers
  moving towards zero) and the gain in precision (ellipses shrinking) are seen together.
* **low-rank views**: `pca()` rotates the coefficients into the principal component space
  of $\mathbf{X}$. There, ridge shrinks each component separately, and most strongly in the
  dimensions with the smallest singular values, which is where the collinearity lives.
* **biplot view**: `biplot()` adds the observed predictors as vectors in the space of the
  smallest dimensions, to show which of them are responsible for the collinearity.

All three depend on $\mathbf{X}$ and one column of $\widehat{\mathbf{B}}(\lambda)$, so for an
`"mlmridge"` object they work one response at a time, selected with `response =`. For
`reading`, @fig-school-pca shows the two ends of the PCA space:

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(pr, variables = 1:2, fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, main = "Dimensions 1 and 2")
plot(pr, variables = 4:5, fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, labels = lab,
     main = "Dimensions 4 and 5")
par(op)
```

### What it does change

What *is* new is the covariance matrix of the coefficients. With
$\mathbf{V}_\lambda = (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}
(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1}$,
$$
\textrm{Var}(\textrm{vec}\, \widehat{\mathbf{B}}(\lambda)) = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \otimes \mathbf{V}_\lambda \; ,
$$
the Kronecker product once more, and for $\lambda = 0$ it's the OLS result
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \otimes (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}$ from the introduction. So the
coefficients of one predictor, for two responses, have covariance matrix
$[\mathbf{V}_\lambda]_{jj} \, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}$: every one of their ellipses has the shape
of the residual covariance matrix, and only the size and center change with $\lambda$.

With `predictor =`, `plot()` shows exactly this view:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (p in c("visit", "counseling"))
  plot(sridge, predictor = p, responses = c("reading", "mathematics"),
       fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, labels = lab)
par(op)
```

This shows two things a univariate view can't. `visit`'s coefficients cross zero for
*both* responses, at nearly the same $\lambda$. And `counseling`'s coefficients move *away* from the origin:
ridge regression shrinks the length of the whole coefficient vector, not each coefficient,
so with correlated predictors some grow while others shrink. The other genuinely new
piece is the choice of $\lambda$. The GCV criterion can be pooled over the responses to
choose one common value, here $\lambda =$ 0.05.

### A design lesson: don't always inherit

My first plan was to give the new object class `c("mlmridge", "ridge")`, so that all of
genridge's existing methods would be inherited. Before committing to that, I built a mock
object and called every inherited method on it. Seven of the twelve stopped with an
error. Viewed generously, that's a good outcome: an error tells you what's wrong. Another
one ran and silently lost the names of the predictors. That is the same "quietly
univariate" problem from the introduction, seen from the developer's side. Good R
developers often learn from this, but don't often confess.

So, in the genridge package `"mlmridge"` became a class of its own. Its methods either handle the matrix of
coefficients directly (`coef()`, `vcov()`, `print()`, `best()`), or delegate to the
univariate method one response at a time through `as.ridge(x, response = )`.

Inheritance is a promise that the parent's methods will do something
sensible with the child. For a model that gains a dimension, it's a promise worth
checking before you make it.

## What's still missing

### `predict.mlm()` with standard errors

Back in the introduction, `predict(fit, se.fit = TRUE)` simply refused. The harder
problem isn't the statistics; it's what `predict()` should give back. For a univariate
model, `predict(..., se.fit = TRUE, interval = "confidence")` returns, for each case, a
fitted value, its standard error, and a confidence interval: `fit`, `se.fit`, `lwr` and
`upr`, each a number. For an `mlm`, every one of these climbs the ladder:

| `predict.lm()` | `lm`: for each case | `mlm`: for each case |
|---|---|---|
| `fit` | $\hat{y}_0$, a number | $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0$, a $q$-vector |
| `se.fit` | a standard error | a $q \times q$ covariance matrix |
| `lwr`, `upr` | an interval | an ellipse (an ellipsoid when $q > 2$) |
| `residual.scale` | $\hat{\sigma}$ | $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, $q \times q$ |

Only `fit` is easy, and base R already does it. The rest follow from the same few lines of
algebra:

* For a new case with predictors $\mathbf{x}_0$, the predicted response vector
is $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0^\top = \mathbf{x}_0^\top \widehat{\mathbf{B}}$, and its covariance
matrix is $h_0 \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, where
$h_0 = \mathbf{x}_0^\top (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_0$ is its leverage.

* The standard error has become a $q \times q$ matrix, and the confidence interval has become
a confidence *ellipse*, with a radius $c$ from Hotelling's $T^2$. In R, with $p$
counting the intercept,
`c2 <- q * (n - p) / (n - p - q + 1) * qf(0.95, q, n - p - q + 1)`.

* For a prediction ellipse, which includes the error for a new case, $h_0$ becomes
$1 + h_0$.

Here's what that looks like for three hypothetical cars, using the `mtcars` model from the
introduction:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
new <- data.frame(hp = c(100, 150, 250), wt = c(2, 3, 4))
X  <- model.matrix(fit)
X0 <- model.matrix(~ hp + wt, new)
n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X); q <- 2
Sigma <- crossprod(residuals(fit)) / (n - p)
h0    <- rowSums((X0 %*% solve(crossprod(X))) * X0)   # leverage of each new case
c2    <- q * (n - p) / (n - p - q + 1) * qf(0.95, q, n - p - q + 1)
yhat  <- predict(fit, new)

plot(qsec ~ mpg, data = mtcars, col = "gray50", pch = 16,
     xlim = c(5, 35), ylim = c(13, 24), asp = 1)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(new))) {
  car::ellipse(yhat[i, ], h0[i] * Sigma, sqrt(c2),
               col = "blue", fill = TRUE, lwd = 2, center.pch = 3)
  car::ellipse(yhat[i, ], (1 + h0[i]) * Sigma, sqrt(c2),
               col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1, center.pch = NULL)
}
```

Every ellipse has the shape of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$; only the size changes. The
figure took a dozen lines. Turning it into a `predict()` method is the part that isn't
settled:

* **`se.fit`.** For $n$ cases, the standard errors become $n$ covariance matrices: an
  $n \times q \times q$ array, or a list of matrices. Since they're all
  $h_0 \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, it could instead return the $n$ leverages and
  $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ once, but then it no longer looks like `predict.lm()`.
* **`lwr` and `upr`.** An ellipse has no lower and upper limits. `predict.lm()` returns
  `cbind(fit, lwr, upr)`, a matrix. A draft in heplots returns an $n \times q \times 3$ array
  of separate bounds for each response, roughly the shadows of the ellipse on each axis.
  These are easy to read, but they throw away the correlation that the ellipse shows.
* **Printing.** Nobody wants to read $n$ covariance matrices.
* **Plotting.** Probably as above, which puts it back in heplots territory.

### Other gaps

`predict()` isn't the only one. A few others, each a case of the same problem:

* **An actual `plot.mlm()`.** R's error message from the introduction still stands. What
  should the default diagnostic plots for an `mlm` be? A $\chi^2$ QQ plot of the residual
  Mahalanobis distances (`cqplot()`), an influence plot and an HE plot would be a start.
  
* **Added-variable plots.** `car::avPlots()` fails on an `mlm`. For a predictor $x_k$, the
  multivariate version would plot the residuals of *all* the responses, adjusted for the other
  predictors, against the residual of $x_k$: $q$ panels, or one panel with a data ellipse for
  each pair of responses. `heplots::pvPlot()` is one step in that direction. It works on a data
  frame, not a model, and shows the conditional relation of *any* two variables, $x$'s or
  $y$'s, given all the others, as a scatterplot of their partial residuals with a data
  ellipse. Plotting $y_j$ against $x_k$, with the other predictors partialled out, gives the
  added-variable plot for one response. Plotting two responses against each other, with all
  the predictors partialled out, shows their residual correlation, the shape of $\mathbf{E}$.
  
* **`car::vif()`.** This one should be easy. VIFs depend only on $\mathbf{X}$, so they're
  the same for every response; `vif()` stops only because it looks for coefficient names
  in a vector, not a matrix.
  
* **Effect displays.** The [effects](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=effects) package plots
  fitted values for each term, with confidence bands [@Fox:03:effects]. For an
  `mlm`, each fitted value is a $q$-vector and each band becomes a set of confidence
  ellipses: the `predict()` problem again, one term at a time.
  
* **Shrinkage that borrows strength across responses.** genridge uses one ridge constant for
  all responses, which leaves each column of $\widehat{\mathbf{B}}$ a univariate ridge.
  Genuinely multivariate shrinkage, as in @Brown-Zidek-1980 or the "curds and whey" method of
  @BreimanFriedman:1997, uses the correlations among the responses, and would need new
  displays of its own.

## Conclusion: what I learned

<!-- MF: a first draft, in your voice. Rework freely. -->

Why write all this down? Partly because these packages grew up one at a time, over
twenty years, and it was only when I lined them up for this post that I saw they were all
solving the same problem. Each time, the response went from $\mathbf{y}$ to
$\mathbf{Y}$, and each time I had to decide what to do with the extra dimension. That
pattern was invisible to me while I was in the middle of it, as I suspect it is for
others writing methods for multivariate models now.

Looking back, a few lessons stand out.

* **The statistics were mostly the easy part.** The theory of the multivariate linear
  model was settled long ago, and much of the computation I needed was already there:
  `car::Anova()` for the $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ matrices, Barrett & Ling's
  influence measures, the Kronecker form of $\textrm{Var}(\textrm{vec}\,\widehat{\mathbf{B}})$.
  The real work was in the software: what a function returns when every object gains a
  dimension, how it prints, and how the methods downstream should consume it.

* **Find the matrix that plays the role of the scalar, then find a way to see it.** A
  variance becomes a covariance matrix, a squared residual a Mahalanobis distance, an
  $F$ ratio the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^{-1}$, a confidence interval an
  ellipse. Once you've named the matrix, the picture is very often an ellipse. That's
  what makes these methods *visual*, and not just multivariate.

* **Not everything needs a new display.** Leverage depends only on $\mathbf{X}$, and so do
  the ridge shrinkage factors and VIFs. Knowing what *doesn't* change is as useful as
  knowing what does, and it keeps the extension honest.

* **The Kronecker product keeps the two dimensions apart.** It turned up again and again:
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \otimes (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}$ for the coefficients in the
  introduction, the metric $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}$
  for Cook's distance, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \otimes \mathbf{V}_\lambda$ for ridge, and
  $h_0 \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, one slice of it, for a predicted value. Each time,
  one factor belongs to the responses and the other to the predictors. That's why leverage
  and VIFs don't change when $\mathbf{y}$ becomes $\mathbf{Y}$, and why the ridge and
  prediction ellipses all have the shape of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$: the extra dimension
  enters through one factor and leaves the other alone.^[The Kronecker product does the same
  tidy bookkeeping on the predictor side. For a full factorial design with one observation
  per cell, in lexicographic order, the model matrix for `y ~ A * B * C` is
  $(\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{X}_A) \otimes (\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{X}_B) \otimes (\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{X}_C)$,
  up to the order of the columns, where each $\mathbf{X}$ holds the contrasts for one factor.
  Replicates add a factor $\otimes \mathbf{1}_n$.]

* **Inheritance is a promise.** S3 dispatch makes it cheap to add an `mlm` method, and an
  `"mlm"` class that inherits from `"lm"` invites every `lm` method to try. Some refuse,
  which is fine. The ones to worry about are those that run and quietly give you $q$
  univariate answers to a multivariate question.

For statisticians, my hope is that this makes the multivariate linear model a little
easier to *see*, not just to fit. For R developers, it's an invitation. The gaps in the
last section, `predict.mlm()` with standard errors, an actual `plot.mlm()`, added-variable
plots and effect displays for multivariate models, are all Un-Vized Problems, with the
statistics in hand and the software still to be written. I'd be glad to hear from anyone
who wants to take one on.

For the longer story, with many more examples, see Chapters 9 and 11--15 of
[_Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in R_](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/).

A. Square, in _Flatland_, could not imagine a third dimension until the Sphere lifted him
out of his plane and showed him one. Most of us learned regression in a world of one
response. Seeing what happens in one more dimension is, I think, worth the trip.
